questions.request:
HL physics, quantum topic. My teacher keeps saying "the photoelectric effect proved light comes in photons" but when I asked HOW physicists actually got convinced she just said "Einstein, 1905". I'm writing this up for a reflection in my physics journal so I need actual evidence and who showed what, not vibes. Can you do these:

(a) Explain, with dates and names, the sequence of experiments and ideas from the first observation of the effect up to the photon idea being accepted. For each person say what they actually measured or claimed (e.g. what exactly did Lenard find, what did Millikan measure, what value of h did he get and how close is it to today's value, when did most physicists actually come round). If any of it is disputed by historians, say who says what rather than just stating it as fact. [6 marks]

(b) Why can't the wave model explain it? Give the three specific observations it fails on, and for the time-delay one use these numbers: work function of sodium 2.28 eV, light intensity 2.0 x 10^-4 W m^-2, assume one atom collects energy over an area of 1.0 x 10^-19 m^2. How long would a classical wave take to deliver the energy to one electron, and what is the measured upper limit on the actual delay? [4 marks]

(c) Our class data for a sodium cathode: f = 6.0 x 10^14 Hz gives stopping voltage 0.20 V; f = 7.5 x 10^14 Hz gives 0.82 V; f = 9.0 x 10^14 Hz gives 1.44 V. Find h, the work function in eV and in J, the threshold frequency and threshold wavelength, and the percentage difference between our h and the accepted value. Show working, not just answers. [5 marks]

(d) My teacher also said Millikan "spent ten years trying to prove Einstein wrong and accidentally proved him right". Is that actually true? Where does that story come from? [2 marks]
strong_answer_must: (a) Give a dated, named sequence with what each person actually did: Hertz 1887 (UV light on spark-gap electrodes made sparks jump more easily, noticed while testing Maxwell's electromagnetic waves); Hallwachs 1888 (a negatively charged zinc plate loses its charge under UV, a positively charged one does not); J. J. Thomson 1899 (the emitted charge carriers have the same charge-to-mass ratio as cathode-ray electrons, so they are electrons); Lenard 1902 (using a retarding/stopping potential: the maximum kinetic energy of photoelectrons does not depend on light intensity but rises with frequency; intensity changes only the number emitted, i.e. the current); Einstein 1905 (Annalen der Physik, the 'heuristic point of view' paper: light energy comes in quanta E = hf, predicting K_max = hf - phi, a straight line of stopping voltage against frequency with slope h/e for every metal); Millikan 1914-1916 (Chicago; sodium, potassium and lithium surfaces cut fresh inside the vacuum with a rotating knife, the 'machine shop in vacuo'; confirmed the straight line and obtained h about 6.57 x 10^-34 J s, i.e. 6.57 x 10^-27 erg s, within roughly 0.5-1% of today's 6.626 x 10^-34 J s; published in Physical Review 1916).

(a) State when acceptance actually came and attribute it: Einstein's light quanta were widely rejected for years (e.g. the 1913 Prussian Academy nomination signed by Planck and others excused his light-quantum hypothesis as having 'missed the target', a well-known quotation that should be attributed as such); Einstein's Nobel Prize for 1921 (awarded 1922) was specifically for 'the law of the photoelectric effect'; Millikan's Nobel 1923; Compton's 1923 X-ray scattering (wavelength shift explained by photon momentum) and the Bothe-Geiger coincidence experiment (1925, against the Bohr-Kramers-Slater statistical proposal of 1924) are usually credited with convincing most physicists; the word 'photon' was coined by G. N. Lewis in 1926. Any claim about what 'most physicists' thought must be hedged and attributed (e.g. 'historians of physics such as ... argue').

(b) Give the three failures of the wave model as specific observations: (1) a threshold frequency below which no electrons are emitted however intense the light; (2) K_max depends on frequency, not intensity, whereas a wave model predicts more intense light gives more energetic electrons; (3) no measurable delay even at very low intensity, whereas a wave must accumulate energy over time.

(b) Worked classical-delay estimate with units: energy needed = 2.28 eV x 1.60 x 10^-19 J/eV = 3.65 x 10^-19 J; power collected per atom = I x A = (2.0 x 10^-4 W m^-2)(1.0 x 10^-19 m^2) = 2.0 x 10^-23 W; t = 3.65 x 10^-19 / 2.0 x 10^-23 = 1.8 x 10^4 s, about 5 hours. Contrast with the measured upper limit: emission within about 10^-9 s (Lawrence and Beams 1928 found no delay greater than about 3 x 10^-9 s), attributed and labelled as the historical bound rather than an exact modern figure.

(c) Working from eV_s = hf - phi: gradient of V_s against f = (1.44 - 0.20) V / (9.0 - 6.0) x 10^14 Hz = 1.24 / 3.0 x 10^14 = 4.13 x 10^-15 V s; this gradient is h/e, so h = 1.60 x 10^-19 x 4.13 x 10^-15 = 6.61 x 10^-34 J s (6.62 x 10^-34 with e = 1.602 x 10^-19). Note or check that the middle point (7.5 x 10^14 Hz, 0.82 V) lies on the same line (4.13 x 10^-15 x 7.5 x 10^14 - 2.28 = 0.82 V).

(c) Work function: phi = h f - e V_s at any point, e.g. 4.13 x 10^-15 V s x 6.0 x 10^14 Hz = 2.48 V, so phi = 2.48 - 0.20 = 2.28 eV = 3.65 x 10^-19 J (consistent with the 2.28 eV used in part (b) and with tabulated sodium values of about 2.3 eV). Threshold frequency f_0 = phi / h = 2.28 eV / 4.13 x 10^-15 eV s = 5.5 x 10^14 Hz; threshold wavelength = c / f_0 = 3.00 x 10^8 / 5.52 x 10^14 = 5.4 x 10^-7 m = 540-545 nm (green; red light would not eject electrons from sodium).

(c) Percentage difference of h from the accepted value, stated with the accepted value used: (6.63 - 6.61) / 6.63 = 0.3% (about 0.1-0.2% if 6.62 x 10^-34 is carried), with the data-booklet value h = 6.63 x 10^-34 J s named as the comparison standard. Consistent use of e = 1.60 x 10^-19 C and correct units throughout (V s for the gradient, J s for h).

(d) Treat the 'ten years to disprove Einstein' story as a contestable historical claim and attribute it: it comes from Millikan's own later accounts (his 1923 Nobel lecture and his 1950 autobiography), and his 1916 Physical Review paper does show him accepting Einstein's equation while calling the light-quantum hypothesis itself untenable or 'bold, not to say reckless' (quotation attributed to Millikan 1916); historians of physics (e.g. Gerald Holton's 1999 centennial essay; also Roger Stuewer) argue the retrospective 'ten years' framing is Millikan's later self-presentation rather than a description of what his 1912-1916 papers were doing. A strong answer says 'partly true, with this origin' and distinguishes the contemporaneous record from the later retelling, rather than asserting either version as fact.

Distinguish Planck 1900 (quantisation of oscillator energy exchange in black-body theory) from Einstein 1905 (quantisation of the light itself), since students often conflate them; avoid saying the effect 'proves light is a particle' and instead state that it is evidence that light exchanges energy in quanta (wave-particle duality).

Marks: if provisional marks are given against the student's [6]/[4]/[5]/[2] allocation, every sentence awarding a mark carries the word 'provisional' and the split is labelled as illustrative, not an official markscheme. A tagged Sources line is present (recalled historical facts must be tagged 'recalled, not consulted', with no URLs).
pitfalls: Date slips presented as fact: Hertz 1888, Lenard 1900 or 1905, Einstein's paper dated 1906, Millikan's measurement dated 1912 or 1921; or saying Einstein's Nobel Prize was for relativity.

Wrong experimental details: saying Millikan used zinc (he used alkali metals, mainly sodium, potassium and lithium) or that he measured e/m; saying Hertz 'discovered the photoelectric effect' in the modern sense without noting he observed only the spark-gap effect; saying Lenard discovered the photon.

Inventing precise quotations, page numbers, journal volumes or exact figures for Millikan's h beyond about 6.57 x 10^-34 J s, or inventing a named historian and a specific book title for the Millikan story; or asserting Millikan's motives as settled fact without attributing the story to his later accounts and to historians' commentary.

Claiming acceptance was immediate after 1905 or after 1916 (it was not: Planck, Bohr and most contemporaries resisted light quanta until Compton 1923 and Bothe-Geiger 1925), or conversely fabricating a specific date when 'everyone accepted' photons.

Calculation errors: treating the gradient of V_s against f as h instead of h/e; mixing eV and J (e.g. reporting phi = 2.28 J); using inconsistent values of e (1.60 vs 1.602) within one calculation without saying so; threshold wavelength arithmetic slips (e.g. 5.4 x 10^-6 m); classical delay slips such as forgetting to convert eV to joules (giving 1.1 x 10^23 s) or using area in cm^2.
Giving a percentage difference without naming the accepted value used, or using an accepted value inconsistent with the data booklet (6.63 x 10^-34 J s).

Stating the 'three observations' vaguely ('intensity does not matter') instead of the specific observed facts each wave-model prediction fails on, or omitting the no-delay observation's measured upper limit.
Conflating Planck's 1900 oscillator quantisation with Einstein's light quanta, or saying Planck proposed photons.
Awarding marks without the word 'provisional' in the same sentence; missing or untagged Sources line; including a URL; stating that recalled historical details were 'consulted'.

questions.request:
Hi, SL physics IA help please. My experiment is the period of a mass bouncing on a spring against the mass. Table 1 below is my raw data and the second thing below is my draft analysis + conclusion section. My teacher gave it back with "intercept??", "is reaction time really the cause?", "uncertainty in k far too small" and "what does the static check actually tell you" written in the margin and I honestly don't get what she wants.

Can you go through it properly: redo the numbers yourself (T and T squared for each mass, the gradient, k, the intercept, and a realistic uncertainty in k with working), then tell me specifically which of my sentences are wrong and why. If the intercept is not reaction time then what is it physically, and can I actually use it for something? Also she said this section is marked on Data analysis and Conclusion (6 marks each) so roughly where would mine sit at the moment? Please don't just say "add more detail", I need to know what is actually wrong. The whole IA has a 3000 word limit so keep the suggestions realistic.

supplied_texts.title: Table 1: raw data, period of a mass on a spring
supplied_texts.text:
Apparatus notes. Spring: steel extension spring, unstretched length 7.2 cm, mass of spring 31 g (weighed on a digital balance, +/-1 g). Masses: slotted masses labelled 100 g each, not weighed. Amplitude: pulled down about 2 cm and released. Timing: digital stopwatch, resolution 0.01 s. 20 oscillations timed, 3 trials for each mass.

mass m / kg | 20T trial 1 / s | 20T trial 2 / s | 20T trial 3 / s
0.100 | 8.41 | 8.28 | 8.35
0.200 | 11.47 | 11.59 | 11.50
0.300 | 14.06 | 13.91 | 14.00
0.400 | 16.03 | 16.18 | 16.07
0.500 | 17.88 | 18.01 | 17.96
0.600 | 19.70 | 19.57 | 19.62

Static check: with 0.300 kg hanging at rest, the extension from the unstretched length was 0.118 m (+/-0.002 m, metre rule).

supplied_texts.title: Draft: Analysis and conclusion section (student's own words)
supplied_texts.text:
Analysis. I averaged the three times for each mass, divided by 20 to get T and squared it. The theory is T = 2 pi sqrt(m/k), so T^2 = (4 pi^2 / k) m, so T^2 against m should be a straight line through the origin with gradient 4 pi^2 / k. Excel gave gradient 1.58 s^2 kg^-1, intercept 0.016 s^2 and R^2 = 0.9999. The intercept should be zero in theory, so it is probably just my reaction time, and I have ignored it. Therefore k = 4 pi^2 / 1.58 = 25.0 N m^-1. The stopwatch reads to 0.01 s, so the uncertainty in each 20T is +/-0.01 s, which makes T uncertain by +/-0.0005 s and k uncertain by about +/-0.03 N m^-1. The static check gave k = (0.300 x 9.81) / 0.118 = 24.9 N m^-1, which is different from 25.0 N m^-1, so one of the two methods must be wrong.

Conclusion. The graph was a straight line with R^2 = 0.9999, which proves that the spring obeys Hooke's law for all masses and that there were no systematic errors in the experiment. My final value is k = 25.0 +/- 0.03 N m^-1. The biggest source of error was reaction time, which is a systematic error because it happened every time I pressed the stopwatch. To improve the experiment I would use a stiffer spring so that the oscillations are slower and easier to time, and a lighter spring so that the intercept disappears.

strong_answer_must: Reprocess the supplied Table 1 explicitly: mean 20T for each mass (8.347, 11.520, 13.990, 16.093, 17.950, 19.630 s), T = mean/20 (0.417, 0.576, 0.700, 0.805, 0.898, 0.982 s) and T^2 (0.174, 0.332, 0.489, 0.647, 0.806, 0.963 s^2), with at least one sample calculation shown.

Confirm the line of best fit of T^2 against m: gradient about 1.58 s^2 kg^-1 (1.578-1.579 by least squares or endpoints), intercept about 0.016 s^2, and k = 4 pi^2 / gradient = 39.5 / 1.58 = 25.0 N m^-1; state that a constant intercept does not change the gradient, so the student's value of k is not invalidated by the intercept.

Identify the intercept physically as the spring's own mass, with the number: effective extra mass = intercept / gradient = 0.016 / 1.58 = 0.010 kg; the student weighed the spring at 31 g, and 31 g / 3 = 10.3 g, matching the one-third-of-spring-mass correction T^2 = (4 pi^2 / k)(m + m_s/3). Attribute and hedge the m_s/3 result: it is an approximation (due to Rayleigh, assuming a uniform spring whose extension varies linearly along its length) valid when the hanging mass is much larger than the spring's mass; so the intercept is evidence for, not proof of, that model, and it can be used (quote the intercept as an estimate of m_s/3 and compare with 31 g/3).

Show why reaction time cannot be the intercept: an intercept of 0.016 s^2 corresponds at m -> 0 to T of about 0.13 s, i.e. about 2.5 s on every 20T reading, far larger than a typical human reaction time of roughly 0.1-0.2 s (labelled as a typical figure); a constant late-stop bias would add to T, not to T^2, and random reaction-time scatter is already visible as the spread between trials, not as an offset. Hence the student's sentence 'it is probably just my reaction time, and I have ignored it' is wrong on two counts.

Replace the uncertainty argument: the stopwatch resolution (0.01 s) is not the dominant uncertainty; the spread of repeats is. Half-range of the three trials is about 0.06-0.075 s in 20T, so T is uncertain by about 0.0035 s (0.8% at 0.100 kg, 0.3% at 0.600 kg), T^2 by about 1.6% at the smallest mass; the slotted masses were not weighed, so their nominal values carry an unknown systematic uncertainty (manufacturer tolerance of order 1%, labelled as typical, not a known figure). Propagate by max-min gradient or percentages to k about 25.0 +/- 0.3 N m^-1 from timing alone, about +/- 0.5 to 0.8 N m^-1 once mass tolerance is included; any justified value in that range is acceptable, and the student's +/- 0.03 is shown to be at least ten times too small, with the final value then quoted to matching precision (e.g. 25.0 +/- 0.5 N m^-1, not 25.0 +/- 0.03).

Evaluate the static check correctly: k_static = (0.300 x 9.81) / 0.118 = 24.9 N m^-1 with fractional uncertainty about 0.002/0.118 = 1.7% (+/- 0.4 N m^-1) plus the same unweighed-mass uncertainty; 24.9 +/- 0.4 and 25.0 +/- 0.5 agree within uncertainty, so 'one of the two methods must have an error' is a non sequitur; the agreement is the evidence that the gradient method is sound and that the intercept is not a problem for k. Optionally note the two methods share the same nominal 0.300 kg mass, so an error in that mass would shift both the same way and the agreement cannot rule it out.

Correct the conclusion's logic: R^2 = 0.9999 measures scatter about the fitted line, not accuracy and not the absence of systematic error; the non-zero intercept is itself a systematic effect; 'proves' should be 'supports' or 'is consistent with'; 'for all masses' extrapolates beyond 0.100-0.600 kg and beyond the elastic limit; the experiment tests the period relation T = 2 pi sqrt(m/k), which assumes Hooke's law rather than directly testing it.

Reclassify reaction time: it is mainly a random uncertainty (varying in size and sign), reduced by timing 20 oscillations and by repeats; only a consistent anticipation bias would be systematic, and that would be small (of order 0.1-0.2 s in 20T, labelled as typical).

Fix the improvement sentence with the physics: a stiffer spring gives shorter periods (T is proportional to 1/sqrt(k)), so 'stiffer so the oscillations are slower' is backwards; realistic, specific improvements are to weigh the slotted masses, include m_s/3 in the model (or use the intercept), use a photogate or motion sensor, and time more oscillations; the student's 'lighter spring' idea is partly right (smaller intercept) but the better fix is to account for the spring mass rather than remove it.

Give band- or mark-level feedback for the two criteria the student named (Data analysis, Conclusion, 6 marks each) with the word 'provisional' in every sentence that gives a mark or band, without claiming to quote official IB descriptor wording, and link each judgement to the specific sentences of the draft that cause it; keep suggestions within the student's 3000-word limit; include a tagged Sources line (supplied text; recalled, not consulted) with no URLs.
pitfalls: Agreeing with the student that the intercept is reaction time, air resistance, or 'experimental error', or explaining it qualitatively without the quantitative link intercept / gradient = 0.010 kg = 31 g / 3.

Getting the spring-mass correction wrong: computing the offset mass as intercept x 4 pi^2 or intercept x k instead of intercept / gradient; stating the correction as m_s/2 or the full m_s; presenting m_s/3 as exact rather than an approximation, or inventing a specific source for it beyond Rayleigh's analysis.
Recomputing the gradient or k incorrectly (e.g. plotting T against m, using 2 pi instead of 4 pi^2, or getting k = 4 pi^2 x gradient = 62 N m^-1).

Endorsing the stopwatch resolution as the uncertainty, or merely saying 'the uncertainty is too small' without deriving a realistic value from the spread of repeats; adding absolute uncertainties where percentages are needed; forgetting to double the percentage uncertainty when squaring T.

Claiming the dynamic and static values of k disagree, or calling 24.9 vs 25.0 an 'error' instead of comparing the difference with the uncertainty; or inventing an 'accepted value' of k for the spring.
Saying R^2 near 1 shows no systematic error, or leaving the 'proves Hooke's law for all masses' claim unchallenged.
Suggesting disproportionate improvements (vacuum chamber, 'more repeats' with no reason) or keeping the backwards 'stiffer spring gives slower oscillations' claim.

Awarding a mark or band without the word 'provisional' in the same sentence; quoting invented official IB descriptor text or the old 2016 criterion names (Personal engagement, Exploration, Analysis, Evaluation, Communication) as if they were the student's criteria.
Fabricating a precise 'manufacturer tolerance' or 'standard reaction time' figure as a known fact rather than a typical order of magnitude.
Missing or untagged Sources line; including a URL; writing the student's section for them rather than correcting the identified sentences.
